title: Nietzsche II: Will to Power, the Übermensch and Eternal Recurrence
subtitle: After the death of God, can we learn to say yes to life?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain Nietzsche's idea of the will to power and why it is not simply a lust for domination
Describe the Übermensch and its opposite, the 'last man,' as presented in Thus Spoke Zarathustra
Explain the thought experiment of eternal recurrence and the attitude of amor fati
Tell the story of how Nietzsche's sister and the Nazis distorted his work, and weigh what in his writing made that possible
Evaluate whether Nietzsche offers a convincing answer to the nihilism he diagnosed
hook:
August 1881. Nietzsche, thirty-six, half-blind and plagued by migraines, is walking beside the lake of Silvaplana near the Swiss village of Sils-Maria, high in the Alps. By a huge pyramid-shaped boulder he stops. A thought has struck him with such force that he later described it as having come to him "6,000 feet beyond man and time." The thought was this: what if everything you have lived, every joy and every pain, every sigh and every trivial moment, would return again, in exactly the same order, infinitely many times?

Yesterday (Day 65) we watched Nietzsche the demolition expert: God is dead, our morality has a shady family history, and nihilism is coming. Many readers stop there and conclude Nietzsche was simply a destroyer. But he saw himself as a physician of culture, someone who had to diagnose the disease before offering a cure. Today we look at that cure, built from four strange and powerful ideas: the will to power, the Übermensch, eternal recurrence and amor fati, the love of fate. And then we look at how those ideas were stolen.

sections.heading: Zarathustra Comes Down the Mountain
sections.body:
Nietzsche presented his positive vision mainly in *Thus Spoke Zarathustra* (1883–85), the strangest book in this course. It is not a treatise but a prophetic prose-poem, written in the style of the Luther Bible, with parables, songs, animals and riddles. Its hero is named after Zarathustra (Zoroaster), the ancient Persian prophet traditionally credited with first teaching that the world is a battle between good and evil. Nietzsche explained in *Ecce Homo* that he chose him precisely because the one who invented that moral error should be the one to overcome it.

At the book's opening, Zarathustra has spent ten years alone in the mountains. Overflowing with wisdom like a cup that wants to run over, he descends to share it. On the way he meets an old hermit in the forest who still sings hymns to God. Walking on, Zarathustra marvels to himself: can it be that this old saint has not yet heard that God is dead?

In a town marketplace he announces his teaching to a crowd gathered to watch a tightrope walker. "I teach you the Übermensch," he proclaims. "Man is something that shall be overcome. What have you done to overcome him?" The crowd laughs. Things go no better when he describes the alternative, and the tightrope walker falls to his death. Zarathustra learns that he must speak not to crowds but to companions.

A warning before we go further: *Zarathustra* is easy to quote and hard to interpret. Nietzsche deliberately wrote in images rather than definitions, and he often said contradictory-seeming things for effect. Scholars disagree about almost every key idea in it. What follows is a fair mainstream reading, but not the only one.

sections.heading: The Will to Power
sections.body:
In *Beyond Good and Evil* (1886) Nietzsche argues that a living thing seeks above all to discharge its strength; life itself, he says, is **will to power**. In *Zarathustra*, in a chapter called "On Self-Overcoming," Zarathustra says that wherever he found the living, he found will to power.

The phrase sounds sinister, as if Nietzsche thought everyone secretly wants to rule the world. But his idea is broader and stranger. Recall Schopenhauer's Will (Day 60): a blind, endless striving underlying everything, which Schopenhauer thought we should try to quiet. Nietzsche keeps the idea of striving but changes its direction. Living things do not merely want to survive, as Darwin's critics sometimes said, nor merely to feel pleasure, as Bentham claimed (Day 61). They want to grow, to expand, to overcome resistance, to express and enhance their strength. Pleasure is the feeling that accompanies increasing power; survival is often merely a side effect.

Power in this sense need not mean power over other people. The artist mastering a difficult technique, the athlete pushing past a limit, the scholar wrestling a problem into order, the person overcoming a bad habit: these are expressions of will to power too. For Nietzsche the highest form is self-overcoming, imposing form and discipline on one's own chaotic drives. He even reinterprets the ascetic priest of yesterday's lesson as someone exercising will to power, by ruling over the suffering and redirecting their ressentiment.

One caution. You may see a book called *The Will to Power* attributed to Nietzsche. He planned a work with that title but abandoned the plan. The book that circulates under that name was assembled after his death by his sister Elisabeth and his friend Heinrich Köselitz (known as Peter Gast) from notebook fragments, arranged according to their choices. Scholars treat it with great caution, and we will see why shortly.

sections.heading: The Übermensch and the Last Man
sections.body:
The **Übermensch** is usually translated "Overman" or "Superman" (George Bernard Shaw popularized the latter in his play *Man and Superman*, and the comic-book hero has no real connection). It names a goal rather than a person who has existed. If God is dead, then meaning can no longer come from above. The Übermensch is the human being who creates meaning and values out of himself, affirms life on earth without needing a heavenly reward, and has overcome both slavish ressentiment and nihilistic despair. Zarathustra puts it in an unforgettable image: man is a rope, tied between beast and Übermensch, a rope over an abyss. What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not an end.

Nietzsche describes the journey in the speech "On the Three Metamorphoses." The spirit first becomes a **camel**, which kneels to take on heavy burdens: duties, traditions, "thou shalt." Then, in the desert, it becomes a **lion**, which fights the great dragon called "Thou shalt" and wins the freedom to say "I will," but cannot yet create new values. Finally it becomes a **child**: innocence, a new beginning, a game, a sacred yes. The child creates.

Far more vivid, and perhaps more relevant to us, is the Übermensch's opposite, the **last man**. When the crowd jeers, Zarathustra describes the most contemptible thing he can imagine: people who have abolished all danger, striving and greatness in favor of comfort. They have their little pleasures for the day and their little pleasures for the night, but they respect their health. Everyone wants the same; everyone is the same. "We have invented happiness," say the last men, and they blink. The crowd's response? "Give us this last man, O Zarathustra!"

This is Nietzsche's nightmare of a post-religious society that avoids nihilism not by creating new values but by giving up on value altogether: a world of safe, contented consumers with no longing to become anything more. Critics note that the Übermensch ideal is deeply elitist. Nietzsche thought most people would never reach it and openly rejected democratic equality, which he saw as slave morality in secular dress. Whether his vision of greatness can be separated from that contempt for ordinary people is a serious question.

sections.heading: Eternal Recurrence: The Greatest Weight
sections.body:
Here is the thought that struck Nietzsche at Sils-Maria, as he presented it in *The Gay Science*, section 341, titled "The Greatest Weight":

Suppose a demon crept after you one day or night into your loneliest loneliness and said: this life, as you now live it and have lived it, you will have to live once more and innumerable times more, with nothing new in it; every pain and every joy, every thought and sigh, even this spider and this moonlight between the trees, all in the same sequence. Would you throw yourself down, gnash your teeth and curse the demon? Or have you ever experienced a tremendous moment when you would answer: you are a god, and never have I heard anything more divine?

This is the doctrine of **eternal recurrence** (or eternal return). Did Nietzsche think it was literally true? In some notebooks he toyed with a cosmological argument: if time is infinite and the number of possible states of matter is finite, every state must eventually repeat. But he never published that argument, and most scholars today read the published version as a *test* or thought experiment rather than physics. Notice that the demon says "suppose."

The test works like this. Kant's categorical imperative (Day 56) asked: could you will your maxim as a universal law? Nietzsche asks: could you will your *life* to recur forever, exactly as it is? If the thought crushes you, that reveals how much you resent your existence and secretly wish it were otherwise, which is the root of nihilism and ressentiment. If you could greet it with joy, you have achieved the most complete possible affirmation of life. It also turns attention to the present: if each moment returns eternally, then each moment carries infinite weight. There is no "real life" waiting somewhere else, in heaven or the future. This is it.

Notice how it reverses Christianity's promise. Christianity offered an eternity that would redeem this life's sufferings. Nietzsche offers an eternity of *this* life, unredeemed, and asks if you can love it anyway.

sections.heading: Amor Fati: Loving Your Fate
sections.body:
Someone who could pass the test of eternal recurrence would have achieved what Nietzsche calls **amor fati**, Latin for "love of fate." In *The Gay Science* (section 276), written for New Year's Day 1882, he resolves to learn more and more to see what is necessary in things as beautiful. Amor fati, he writes, let that be my love from now on. He adds that he does not want to wage war against what is ugly or to accuse anyone, not even the accusers: looking away shall be his only negation. Someday he wishes to be only a Yes-sayer. In *Ecce Homo* (written 1888) he calls amor fati his formula for greatness in a human being: that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.

This is not passive resignation. Remember the Stoics (Days 25 and 26), who taught us to accept what is outside our control. Nietzsche admired them but thought their acceptance had a grim, tight-lipped quality, like enduring bad weather. Amor fati goes further: not merely to bear what is necessary, still less to conceal it, but to *love* it. Even the suffering? Especially the suffering, insofar as it shaped who you are. From *Twilight of the Idols* comes the line that has become a cliché: what does not kill me makes me stronger. Nietzsche, who lived with constant pain, meant it seriously. His illness, he claimed, taught him to see from many perspectives and gave him his philosophy.

How do the four ideas fit together? The will to power describes what life fundamentally is: striving and self-overcoming. The death of God removes external sources of meaning. The Übermensch is the ideal of a human being who creates meaning through that striving. And eternal recurrence with amor fati is the test and the attitude of total affirmation that such a person would embody. Together they are Nietzsche's answer to nihilism: not a new God or a new system, but a way of saying yes to this life, here, with nothing held back. A question to keep in mind for Camus (Day 79), who imagined Sisyphus happy: is that a profound answer or a heroic pose?

sections.heading: Stolen Ideas: The Nazis and Nietzsche's Sister
sections.body:
Few philosophers have been more abused after death. The central figure is Nietzsche's sister, **Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche** (1846–1935). In 1885 she married Bernhard Förster, a prominent antisemitic agitator, and they founded a colony of "pure" Germans called Nueva Germania in the jungle of Paraguay. Nietzsche despised the marriage. In letters he insisted on being unequivocally opposed to antisemitism and told his sister that her husband's cause repeatedly filled him with anger or melancholy; he had already broken with Wagner partly over Wagner's antisemitism and German nationalism, which he repeatedly mocked. The colony failed and Förster killed himself in 1889.

Elisabeth returned to Germany just as her brother collapsed. She took control of his manuscripts and his growing fame, founded the Nietzsche Archive, eventually in Weimar, wrote a sanitized biography, edited his letters (including some outright forgeries) and assembled *The Will to Power* from his notebooks. She presented him as a prophet of German nationalism. In the 1930s she welcomed the Nazis; Hitler visited the Archive, and when she died in 1935 he attended her funeral. Nazi propagandists quoted phrases like "will to power," "master morality" and "blond beast" out of context to dress up their ideology.

After the war, scholars such as Walter Kaufmann and the editors Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, who produced a reliable critical edition of his writings, worked to recover the real Nietzsche: an anti-nationalist who called himself a "good European," an enemy of antisemites and a fierce critic of the German state's worship of power.

But honesty requires more than a rescue story. Nietzsche did write things that made misuse easy. He praised hardness and cruelty in the noble type, spoke of breeding a higher humanity, despised democracy and socialism, wrote contemptuously about women, and his account of the slave revolt in morality uses Jewish history polemically. His notorious "blond beast" in the *Genealogy* refers to the lion and to many aristocratic peoples, Roman, Arab, Germanic, Japanese, Homeric, not to a race; yet the image was ripe for abuse. The fair verdict is that the Nazis distorted Nietzsche badly, and that his work also contains elitist and dangerous strands that readers must confront rather than explain away. Sadly, Heidegger (Day 76) will give us another case study in how philosophy and Nazism became entangled.

keyQuote.text: My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.
keyQuote.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ecce Homo (written 1888), 'Why I Am So Clever,' section 10 (trans. Walter Kaufmann)

modernConnection.title: "What Doesn't Kill You" and the Gospel of Self-Optimization
modernConnection.body:
Nietzsche is everywhere in contemporary self-help, usually without his name. "What doesn't kill you makes you stronger" became a pop anthem for Kelly Clarkson; "become who you are," the subtitle idea of *Ecce Homo*, which Nietzsche borrowed from the Greek poet Pindar, appears on gym walls and in productivity podcasts. Psychologists studying post-traumatic growth have found that many people report positive changes after adversity, such as deeper relationships, a new sense of priorities and greater personal strength. That is close to amor fati's claim that suffering can become part of a life worth affirming.

The Übermensch has a more literal modern descendant in transhumanism, the movement that seeks to use technology, genetics and artificial intelligence to overcome human limits of intelligence, lifespan and even death. Some transhumanist writers explicitly cite Nietzsche's line that man is something to be overcome.

The last man may be even more relevant. Zarathustra's picture of a society that has "invented happiness," with little pleasures for the day and for the night, no longings and no risks, reads to many critics like a description of a comfortable consumer culture of streaming, snacks and wellness apps. The political theorist Francis Fukuyama devoted the final part of *The End of History and the Last Man* (1992) to this worry: that liberal democracy might produce contented people without greatness.

But Nietzsche would probably sneer at most of his modern fans. Hustle culture measures self-overcoming in followers, income and muscle mass, which are exactly the herd's standards. Post-traumatic growth research also shows that suffering often simply harms people; trauma does not reliably make anyone stronger, and telling sufferers that it should can add shame to pain. Transhumanism's focus on enhancing capacities through technology misses Nietzsche's emphasis on creating *values*, not just abilities. The test of eternal recurrence is not "would this life look good on social media?" but "could I will every moment of it, including the unglamorous ones, again and again?"

vocabulary.definition: Nietzsche's name for the basic drive of all life: not mere survival or pleasure, but growth, expansion, overcoming resistance and, at its highest, self-overcoming.
vocabulary.example: A pianist practicing a passage for the hundredth time until she masters it is, for Nietzsche, expressing will to power.

vocabulary.definition: The 'Overman': Nietzsche's ideal of a human being who creates his or her own values and fully affirms earthly life after the death of God.
vocabulary.example: Zarathustra describes humanity as a rope stretched between beast and Übermensch.

vocabulary.definition: Nietzsche's image of the contemptible endpoint of a culture that has given up striving and greatness for safe, uniform comfort.
vocabulary.example: 'We have invented happiness,' say the last men, and they blink.

vocabulary.definition: Zarathustra's parable of the spirit's development: the camel that bears burdens, the lion that wins freedom by defeating 'Thou shalt,' and the child that creates new values.
vocabulary.example: In the three metamorphoses, the lion can say 'I will' but only the child can create.

vocabulary.definition: The thought that one's life will repeat infinitely in exactly the same sequence, used by Nietzsche chiefly as a test of whether one can affirm life completely.
vocabulary.example: Facing the idea of eternal recurrence, she asked herself whether she would gladly relive even her worst year.

vocabulary.definition: Latin for 'love of fate': the attitude of wanting nothing to be different, not merely accepting but loving what is necessary in one's life.
vocabulary.example: Rather than regretting his illness, Nietzsche practiced amor fati, crediting it with sharpening his thought.

vocabulary.definition: The disciplined shaping and surpassing of one's own drives and limitations, which Nietzsche regarded as the highest form of will to power.
vocabulary.example: Quitting a long-time addiction is a powerful example of self-overcoming.

vocabulary.definition: The institution founded by Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche to control her brother's papers, which spread a distorted, nationalist image of him and later welcomed the Nazis.
vocabulary.example: Scholars had to work around editions produced by the Nietzsche Archive to recover what Nietzsche actually wrote.

thinkingExercise.title: The Demon's Question
thinkingExercise.prompt: Take Nietzsche's thought experiment seriously for 10 to 15 minutes. Find a quiet spot and imagine the demon of The Gay Science, section 341, whispering to you.
steps: Write your immediate, honest reaction to the idea of living your life exactly as it has been, infinitely many times. Horror? Joy? Indifference?
List three moments you would gladly relive forever, and three you would dread. What do the dreaded ones have in common?
Choose one of the dreaded moments and try amor fati: can you see how it contributed to who you are or what you value? Is loving it possible, or would that be dishonest?
Now turn the test forward: what one change in how you live next month would make your life more worth repeating?
Critique: is eternal recurrence a fair test? Write a short paragraph on whether someone who has suffered severe trauma or injustice should be asked to affirm it.

summary: Thus Spoke Zarathustra presents Nietzsche's positive vision in poetic, prophetic form, and is notoriously open to interpretation.
The will to power is the drive of life to grow and overcome resistance, most highly as self-overcoming; it is not simply a desire to dominate others.
The Übermensch is the ideal of a human being who creates values and affirms earthly life after the death of God; its opposite is the comfortable, aspiration-free last man.
Eternal recurrence asks whether you could will your life to repeat forever; amor fati is the love of fate that would answer yes.
Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche and the Nazis distorted his work, which he would have rejected in its antisemitic and nationalist forms, though his elitism and harsh rhetoric made misuse easier.

quiz.question: How is Nietzsche's will to power best understood?
options: As the desire of every individual to rule over other people
As the basic drive of life to grow, overcome resistance and, at its highest, overcome itself
As the same thing as Schopenhauer's will, which should be silenced
As the desire for pleasure and the avoidance of pain
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche keeps Schopenhauer's idea of striving but affirms it, and he rejects both bare survival and pleasure as life's fundamental aim.

quiz.question: The book published as The Will to Power is a finished work that Nietzsche completed and prepared for publication himself.
quiz.explanation: It was compiled after his death by his sister and Peter Gast from notebook fragments, and scholars use it cautiously.

quiz.question: In the speech 'On the Three Metamorphoses,' which figure creates new values?
options: The camel
The lion
The dragon
The child
quiz.explanation: The camel bears burdens, the lion wins freedom by defeating 'Thou shalt,' but only the child, as a new beginning and sacred yes, creates.

quiz.question: A society where people have abolished risk and ambition, enjoy small daily comforts, all want the same things and claim to have 'invented happiness' best matches which Nietzschean image?
options: The last man
The Übermensch
Master morality
The knight of faith
quiz.explanation: Zarathustra's 'last men' are complacent, uniform and comfortable, the opposite of the striving Übermensch.

quiz.question: How do most scholars read the eternal recurrence passage in The Gay Science, section 341?
options: As a proven law of physics
As a description of Christian heaven
Primarily as a thought experiment that tests whether one can affirm one's life
As a prediction that history moves through dialectical stages
quiz.explanation: The passage begins with 'suppose' a demon said this; Nietzsche toyed with a cosmological version only in unpublished notes.

quiz.question: How does amor fati differ from Stoic acceptance, as Nietzsche saw it?
options: Amor fati rejects whatever is necessary
Amor fati means not just enduring what is necessary but loving it
Amor fati is identical to the Stoic dichotomy of control
Amor fati requires belief in a providential God
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche admired Stoic endurance but wanted something more: wanting nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.

quiz.question: Nietzsche approved of his sister's marriage to the antisemitic activist Bernhard Förster.
quiz.explanation: He despised the marriage and antisemitism generally, telling his sister that her husband's antisemitic cause filled him with anger or melancholy.

quiz.question: What is the best summary of the relationship between Nietzsche and Nazism?
options: Nietzsche was an active member of the Nazi Party
Nietzsche's writings contain nothing that could be misused
The Nazis had no interest in Nietzsche
The Nazis distorted his work, aided by his sister, though his elitist and harsh rhetoric made such misuse easier
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche died in 1900, long before the party existed. He opposed antisemitism and German nationalism, but honesty requires admitting troubling strands in his writing.

quiz.question: Nietzsche's ideal of the Übermensch was egalitarian: he expected all people to reach it through democratic reforms.
quiz.explanation: Nietzsche was openly elitist and anti-democratic, believing only rare individuals could create new values.

quiz.question: How do Nietzsche's four positive ideas fit together as a response to nihilism?
options: They describe life as striving, propose a value-creating ideal, and offer a test and attitude of total affirmation of this life
They prove that God exists after all
They show that pleasure is the only good
They argue that the state should define values for its citizens
quiz.explanation: Will to power describes life, the Übermensch is the ideal, eternal recurrence is the test and amor fati is the affirming attitude, together answering the threat of meaninglessness.

goDeeper.body:
Eternal recurrence has generated a fascinating debate. If it is meant literally, critics point out a puzzle: if my next life is an exact repetition with no memory of this one, in what sense is it *me* who returns, and why should I care? Compare the puzzles of personal identity from Locke (Day 47) and Hume (Day 50). Bernd Magnus and Alexander Nehamas instead read recurrence as a test of attitude. Nehamas, in *Nietzsche: Life as Literature*, offers an especially striking reading: Nietzsche's insight is that everything about a life is so interconnected that wanting to change any one thing would mean wanting to be a different person. To affirm yourself at all is to affirm all of it, as a novelist must accept every scene that makes a character who she is. On this view Nietzsche's ideal is to live one's life like a well-made work of art.

Others worry this makes ethics purely aesthetic. Can a life of brilliant, coherent cruelty pass the test? Nietzsche's defenders argue that someone driven by cruelty is usually acting from ressentiment and could not genuinely affirm life, while critics reply that this is wishful thinking.

A second debate concerns the will to power. Is it a metaphysical claim about all reality (as Heidegger thought), a psychological hypothesis about human motivation, or a standard of value, telling us to judge values by whether they enhance life? Nietzsche's published works support each reading in different places. Finally, it is worth reading the third part of Zarathustra, 'On the Vision and the Riddle,' where recurrence is presented through the image of a gateway called 'Moment,' with an eternal lane running backward and one running forward.

readings.title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
readings.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (trans. R.J. Hollingdale or Graham Parkes)
readings.note: Read the Prologue and 'On the Three Metamorphoses'; then 'On the Vision and the Riddle' for recurrence.

readings.title: I Am Dynamite! A Life of Nietzsche
readings.author: Sue Prideaux
readings.note: A vivid, prize-winning biography that covers Elisabeth, Paraguay and the Nazi appropriation in detail.

readings.title: Nietzsche: Life as Literature
readings.author: Alexander Nehamas
readings.note: An influential and readable interpretation of eternal recurrence and self-creation.

readings.title: Forgotten Fatherland: The Search for Elisabeth Nietzsche
readings.author: Ben Macintyre
readings.note: A journalist's account of Nueva Germania and Elisabeth's role in shaping her brother's reputation.

questions: Is the Übermensch an inspiring ideal of self-creation, or an elitism that cannot be separated from contempt for ordinary people?
Could someone pass the test of eternal recurrence and still be a bad person? What would that tell us about Nietzsche's ethics?
When a philosopher's work is misused, how much responsibility does the philosopher bear?
